planting.note: Set out container divisions in spring once soil has warmed, in fertile, well-drained soil; as a true clumping bamboo it has tight rhizomes and needs no barrier, unlike running Phyllostachys types.

directions: Golden Goddess is a compact, dense-clumping selection of hedge bamboo prized for its arching, weeping habit and slender golden-green culms, making it one of the most popular low-screening bamboos for Gulf Coast and Florida landscapes. Plant divisions in enriched, well-drained soil and water deeply while establishing; once rooted it tolerates heat and moderate drought with only occasional irrigation. Because it stays under 12-15 feet and forms a tight, non-spreading clump, it works well close to foundations, pools, or property lines where an invasive runner would be a liability. Cut out old, thinning culms at ground level each spring to keep the clump dense and encourage fresh growth.

common_name: Fernleaf Bamboo (Chinese Goddess Bamboo, Tiny Fern Bamboo)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to filtered sun; this dwarf form stays small enough for large containers and border edges.

directions: This is the smallest commonly grown Bambusa multiplex cultivar, with tiny, fern-like leaves clustered densely along wiry culms, giving the whole plant a soft, feathery texture unlike any other clumping bamboo. It stays under 8 feet and forms a tight, non-invasive clump, making it a favorite for foundation plantings, tight side yards, and large patio pots in warm climates. Provide dappled shade in the hottest part of the day, especially inland, since foliage can scorch in full Gulf Coast summer sun. Thin out old culms occasionally at the base to maintain its naturally graceful, mounding form.

planting.note: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in a site with afternoon shade; this cold-hardy clumper performs best where summers are not extremely hot and humid.

directions: Green Panda bamboo is one of the most shade- and cold-tolerant clumping bamboos available, forming a dense, arching thicket of slender green culms that stays reliably non-invasive thanks to its tight pachymorph rhizome system. It is widely planted under high tree canopy or on the shaded north side of buildings where running bamboos would be unwelcome, and it takes winter cold to roughly -10 to -20°F once established. In the Deep South and other hot, humid regions it appreciates consistent moisture and afternoon shade, since Fargesia species generally sulk in prolonged summer heat compared to tropical clumping bamboos. Mulch well and avoid letting the shallow root zone dry out during establishment.

common_name: Henon Bamboo (Giant Timber Form of Black Bamboo)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; being a running bamboo it requires an 18-24 inch deep rhizome barrier to contain spread.

directions: Henon is a large-culm selection of black bamboo grown for timber-scale poles rather than dark color; unlike the straight species its mature culms stay green to grayish-green rather than turning black, and it grows considerably taller and thicker, making it the preferred choice where sturdy poles or a dramatic upright grove effect is wanted. It runs by rhizome like other Phyllostachys, so a physical barrier or regular trenching is essential to keep it from escaping into lawns or neighboring beds. Feed young groves with a balanced or nitrogen-rich fertilizer in spring to speed culm size increase over the first several growing seasons. Once established it tolerates heat, humidity, and occasional flooding, and thins naturally into a graceful, high-canopied grove if older culms are selectively removed.

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; established clumps are drought-tolerant but look best with regular water through the first two seasons.

directions: This subtropical clumping bamboo produces extremely fine-textured, blue-green foliage on thin culms that arch gracefully outward in a fountain-like habit, giving it a soft, willowy look unlike any timber bamboo. It is a true clumper with tight rhizomes, so it never becomes invasive and is a popular specimen or screening plant around pools and patios in Florida, coastal California, and the Gulf South. It tolerates poor, rocky soil once established but grows fastest and fullest with occasional deep watering and a light annual feeding. Foliage can be damaged by hard freezes, but established clumps generally resprout from the base after cold snaps in zone 8b-9 gardens.

common_name: Spectabilis Bamboo (Golden Culm Selection of Yellow Groove Bamboo)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun for best culm color; install a deep rhizome barrier before planting since this is a running bamboo.

directions: Spectabilis is a striking sport of yellow groove bamboo with culms that turn brilliant golden-yellow with a random green stripe on one side, plus the characteristic zigzagged lower internodes shared by the species, making it one of the most colorful cold-hardy bamboos in cultivation. It is exceptionally winter-hardy for a Phyllostachys, tolerating temperatures well below zero once established, and colors best with full sun exposure. As a running bamboo it needs a barrier or annual rhizome pruning to stay contained, but it rewards the effort with a fast-growing, dramatically colored grove useful for screening or as a striking specimen planting. New shoots are edible when harvested young, similar to other Phyllostachys species.

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container bushes in fall or late winter in cool, moisture-retentive soil; this early-season Dutch cultivar benefits from a site sheltered from late spring frost during bloom.

directions: Jonkheer van Tets is a classic early-ripening red currant valued for its long, uniform strigs of bright red, tart-sweet berries that ripen ahead of most other red currant cultivars, extending the harvest window when grown alongside later types like Rovada or Red Lake. It sets fruit heavily and reliably, but the early bloom period makes it vulnerable to late spring frosts, so a site with some air drainage or light overhead protection during flowering helps secure the crop. Grow in cool, humus-rich, well-drained soil with consistent moisture, and prune out the oldest third of the wood each dormant season on an open, vase-shaped framework to maintain fruiting vigor. It performs best in regions with cool summers and struggles in hot, humid climates.

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring in fertile, moisture-retentive soil; set the crown slightly below grade to encourage multiple basal shoots for a productive bush.

directions: Wellington XXX is a heritage English black currant cultivar dating to the early 20th century, still grown for its heavy, reliable yields of large, richly flavored, dark berries well suited to jams, syrups, and cordials. It is a vigorous, spreading bush that produces well even in cooler, shorter-season climates, and its mid-season ripening helps spread the harvest when grown with earlier or later black currant selections. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, mulch to conserve moisture, and prune out about a quarter of the oldest wood each winter to stimulate new fruiting canes, since black currants fruit best on one- and two-year-old growth. Watch for reduced vigor and yield in hot-summer regions, as this cultivar performs best where summers stay relatively cool.
